technique: verbs over adjectives — how the action words carry the weight
lesson: Today we work on verbs. A verb is an action word. It tells you what something does. This poem uses verbs to carry the weight, instead of leaning on describing words. Look at the crow: it "goes over" and it's "dragging its voice across the stubbled field." The word "dragging" does the work. You hear effort and roughness because that verb shows effort. Later the frost "has laid its thin glass on the glass." "Laid" makes it an action, something placed, not just a flat fact. Verbs keep the poem moving. They make you picture something happening in time, so your attention follows it. A pile of adjectives sits still. A strong verb pulls you forward. Try this: write a sentence about one thing, then cut every describing word and make the verb do the job instead. The second time through, listen only for the action words and how each one moves you to the final push. Here is the poem.
poem:
A crow goes over, two rough notes and done,
dragging its voice across the stubbled field
like something heavy pulled over gravel.
You lie there counting what the day will hold—
a letter to send that steadies someone's hand,
a nervous question to answer soft and plain,
the slow arithmetic of what's enough.
Frost has laid its thin glass on the glass,
and through it the light comes gray and honest,
asking nothing yet. The floor is cold.
Downstairs the stove's gone low but not gone out.

The coffee's still where you left it, the quiet's still yours for an hour—nobody needs you to be anything yet but awake.

So — up!
